articles.title: ₱17.8B set aside for undernourished learners next year, says Libanan
articles.description: The nutrition of undernourished learners in public schools and day care centers is a ₱17.8-billion effort next year based on earmarked amounts in the proposed ₱7.2-trillion 2027 national budget. This was revealed by House Minority Leader and 4Ps Party-list Rep. Marcelino “Nonoy” Libanan said Monday, Nov. 2, as the country marked the start of National Children’s Month. Under the proposed 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP), the sum of ₱11.4 billion has been earmarked for the School-Based Feeding Program (SBFP), while another ₱6.4 billion is allocated for the Supplementary Feeding Program (SFP), according to Libanan. “As members of Congress, we have a duty to ensure that public funds are spent wisely and that people know where their money is going, especially when it comes to programs that directly affect social welfare,” Libanan said. He said Congress has a responsibility not only to scrutinize government spending but also to inform citizens how public funds are being used, particularly for programs that directly benefit vulnerable sectors. The ₱7.2-trillion General Appropriations Bill (GAB)--the legislative equivalent of the NEP--was approved on third and final reading by the House of Representatives last month. The Philippines observes National Children’s Month every November, highlighting the importance of protecting children’s rights and promoting their health, nutrition and overall well-being. The United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, adopted on November 20, 1989, recognizes every child’s right to health, adequate nutrition, education and protection. “We must treat proper nutrition as an essential investment in our children’s future. A child who goes to school hungry faces greater difficulty concentrating, participating in class and keeping up with lessons,” Libanan said. “By ensuring that nutritious food reaches children who need it most, these feeding programs can help remove hunger as a barrier to learning and give our young people a stronger foundation to grow and develop,” he added. The need for sustained government intervention comes amid persistent reports of hunger among Filipino families. A Social Weather Stations (SWS) survey found that 20.3 percent of families experienced involuntary hunger—being hungry and having nothing to eat—at least once in the second quarter of 2026. A separate OCTA Research survey reported that self-rated hunger rose to 21 percent in July from 17 percent in March. The SBFP provides nutritious meals to incoming kindergarten learners and pupils in Grades 1 to 6 identified as wasted, severely wasted, stunted or severely stunted. It also covers learners at risk of dropping out as well as children from indigenous communities and indigent households. Meanwhile, the SFP provides nutritious meals to preschool children enrolled in public child development centers, as well as children participating in supervised neighborhood play activities. The SBFP and the SFP are administered by the Department of Education (DepEd) and the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), respectively. Libanan said the government should maximize the impact of feeding programs by sourcing food supplies, whenever possible, from local farmers and dairy producers. “This will allow us to address child malnutrition while supporting Filipino growers,” he said.

articles.title: Humanitarian Crisis Unfolds In Gaza As Hunger , Disease Grip the Strip - BW Healthcare World
articles.description: In a devastating turn of events, hunger is tightening its grip on the Gaza Strip, with dire consequences predicted for the health of the population, especially among vulnerable groups such as children, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and the elderly, WHO said in its recent statement. Recent estimates from the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) global partnership, which includes the World Health Organization (WHO), reveal alarming levels of food insecurity in Gaza. The risk of famine looms larger each day, underscoring the urgent need for immediate intervention. An unprecedented 93 per cent of Gaza's population is now grappling with crisis-level hunger, characterised by insufficient food and alarming rates of malnutrition. Shockingly, at least one in four households is facing what experts term "catastrophic conditions" — extreme lack of food leading to desperation, starvation, and resorting to extreme measures, such as selling possessions, just to secure a basic meal. The consequences are dire, with visible signs of starvation, destitution, and, tragically, death.WHO staff on recent missions to north Gaza report a heartbreaking scenario , every person they encountered, including those in hospitals and emergency wards, is hungry. The desperation is so profound that people rush towards medical supply trucks, hoping for food. In the midst of this humanitarian crisis, infectious diseases are on the rise, further exacerbating the suffering. Since mid-October, over 100,000 cases of diarrhoea have been reported, with half affecting children under the age of 5 , a 25-fold increase compared to pre-conflict levels. In addition, more than 150,000 cases of upper respiratory infections, along with instances of meningitis, skin rashes, scabies, lice, and chickenpox, have been documented. Suspected cases of hepatitis are emerging, evident in individuals presenting with jaundice. The weakened state of hunger-stricken bodies makes them susceptible to diseases that a healthy body could more easily fend off. Malnutrition, particularly among children, increases the risk of death from illnesses like diarrhoea, pneumonia, and measles, especially in an environment where access to life-saving health services is severely limited. Even if children survive, the long-term consequences of malnutrition can stunt growth and impair cognitive development, WHO said. Breastfeeding mothers, crucial for the well-being of infants, are also at high risk of malnutrition. The lack of access to safe drinking water heightens the vulnerability of both mothers and infants to deadly diseases such as diarrhoea. Compounding the crisis is the lack of sanitation and hygiene in Gaza, exacerbated by a collapsing health system. With over 1.9 million people displaced, living in overcrowded shelters, the conditions are ripe for the continued spread of infectious diseases. Access to health services has drastically declined amid the ongoing conflict, leaving those grappling with the dual challenges of hunger and disease with limited options. The people of Gaza, already burdened by years of conflict, now face the looming threat of death from starvation and preventable diseases. Urgent action is imperative. Increased humanitarian aid, particularly in the form of food and medical assistance, is crucial. WHO reiterates its call for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire to alleviate the suffering of the Gazan population.
